newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels deny relaxing negotiating stance.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels deny relaxing negotiating stance.

text.p: Marxist guerrillas holding 72 VIP hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence said on Thursday they were not giving up their main demand for the release of some 400 comrades in Peruvian jails.

The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas said reports they would settle instead for ransom payments, improved prison conditions and asylum in a foreign country for themselves were "lies" spread by the government.

Such versions "only seek to confuse the objectives (of the takeover) and obstruct a political solution," the MRTA said in a statement sent to Reuters by e-mail from its international spokesman Isaac Velazco in Hamburg, Germany.

The roughly 15 rebels who stormed the residence on Dec. 17 have consistently demanded the release of all jailed MRTA members. President Alberto Fujimori has repeatedly ruled out considering that demand.

But the recent renewal of face-to-face talks between the two sides after weeks of mutual intransigence prompted speculation the MRTA might have privately expressed a willingness to negotiate its principal demand.

One MRTA leader told Reuters in an interview in the group's jungle stronghold that they might be prepared to accept the release of a smaller number of prisoners, depending on their experience or importance in the movement.

Government negotiator Domingo Palermo and MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa began a seventh round of talks at around 4.30 p.m. (2130 GMT) on Thursday afternoon aimed at negotiating a bloodless end to the siege now in its 72nd day.

As a Red Cross car drove Cerpa to the talks in a safe house across the street from the residence, his fellow rebels broadcast their revolutionary hymn commemmorating dead comrades and shouted defiant slogans.
"What is our mission? Freedom for the prisoners! On the 72nd day of the hostage-taking, nobody surrenders, damn it!" they shouted.

After the last round of talks on Tuesday, guarantors overseeing the talks issued a statement saying only that the two sides had met "in the same atmosphere" as in prior meetings, which they had described as "constructive."
The MRTA leader said in the jungle interview that time was on the rebels' side and they were prepared to wait as long as necessary for a "dignified solution to the siege."

"We are in no hurry," the rebel, who identified himself as Comrade Alejandro, a member of the MRTA's high command, said at a secret training camp. "What do we lose if we wait months, when we have waited centuries for a revolution?"

As the talks continued, Congress President Victor Joy Way said lawmakers have before them six proposals to create a panel to investigate why Peru's security forces failed to prevent the MRTA from seizing the diplomatic compound.
And police chiefs met to begin an internal investigation into police responsibility for the guerrilla strike, according to the daily La Republica.

The MRTA's statement on Thursday called for Argentine human rights group Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo to mediate in the crisis. "Their presence in the negotiations is of vital importance to ensure against the unnecessary bloodshed that the government desires," it said.

Fujimori has said he will use force only if harm is done to the remaining captives, who include his brother, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia, two government ministers and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
